quotes.quote: Assume a seated position on a leg press machine angled at approximately a 45º angle.
Place your feet against the resistance platform with your hips and spine against the back support.
Your feet should be shoulder width apart and placed in the middle of the resistance platform. Pressure should be felt on the entire soles of both feet.
Position your feet on the platform hip-width apart with your knees bent at approximately 90 degrees.
Release the locking lever located on the sides of the seat and then straighten the legs.
Push the platform away with your feet and disengage the safety side handles by turning them (usually) outwards. The handles are levers that release and lock the footplate in place.
Place your hands on the handles for stability and release the safety bars.
The legs should be fully extended but not locked and the trunk should be held firmly against the back support. This is the starting position.
Continue extending your hips and knees until the knees reach a relaxed, extended position, with the heels still pressed firmly into the plate.
Do not hyperextend (lock-out) your knees and avoid lifting your butt off the seat pad or rounding out your low back.
Then, push the footplate back up until your legs are almost straight again. Don't lock out your knees completely.
Bend your legs until there is an 80-90? angle in the knees (measured from the back of the shin to the back of the thigh).
Lower the platform back toward your body with control, returning to approximately 90 degrees of knee flexion.
adjust your seat and foot position so that the bend in your knees is at approximately 90 degrees with your heels flat.
In one leg, the knee flexion range of motion (ROM) was fixed at approximately 5-100°, while for the other leg, participants used their maximum individualized ROM (5-154 ± 7.8°).

These findings suggest that both knee flexion ROMs are similarly effective for promoting quadriceps femoris muscle hypertrophy over a relatively short training-period in resistance-trained individuals.
Twenty-three participants (training age: 7.2 ± 3.5 years) completed a within-participant design, performing four sets of unilateral leg presses to momentary failure twice weekly for 8 weeks.
Leg press machines commonly cause low back injury because of the rounding of the back when the knees are close to the chest.
The closer the knees get to the chest, the greater is the rounding in the lower back which puts pressure on the lumbar intravertebral discs and can cause injury.
Do not allow your upper thighs to compress your ribcage.
Descending too far beyond 90 degrees of knee flexion, which reduces control
Improper technique can lead to injury. Control the extension phase by keeping your heels in contact with the plate and avoid locking out your knees.

Be sure that you do not lock out the knees at the end of the movement, especially if you naturally have several degrees of hyperextension in the locked position. This can lead to excessive hyperextension, which can severely injure the knees.
Locking out knees at full extension, which removes tension and stresses the joint
The risk of knee dislocation can be reduced by avoiding locking and hyperextension of the knees during any type of leg press or squatting exercise.
Allowing knees to cave inward (valgus), which indicates poor motor control
Using excessive weight that compromises form or allows knees to collapse inward
Sit in the machine, positioning your back and sacrum (tailbone) flat against the machine's backrest.
Contract (“brace”) your abdominal muscles to stabilize your spine, be careful to avoid movement in your low back throughout the exercise.
Sit on the leg press machine with your back and head firmly against the backrest.
Lightly grasp any available handles to stabilize your upper extremity.
Inhale slightly more than usual and hold your breath as you bend (flex) the legs to lower the platform.
Exhale as you pass the most difficult part of the upward pressing action.
Slowly exhale while pushing the resistance plate away from your body by contracting your glutes, quadiceps and hamstrings.
